idiom_name: sorted [(start: Date, value: T)] array + hand-written lower bound
implementation_notes: Foundation gives the Time Point (Date as an absolute instant, Calendar/DateComponents for calendar arithmetic, DateInterval for spans) but no ordered map with a floor lookup, so the milestone store is an array sorted by effective date with a hand-written lower-bound search (or last(where:) for short histories) and the owner exposes salary(at:) plus a default form that reads a Date once. What replaces the classic structure: nothing, beyond DateInterval standing in for the hand-rolled (from, to) pair and value-type semantics making stored versions immutable for free. Keep this form when the history lives in the app or comes from a server that returns version rows; when the store is a relational system-versioned table, the as-of read belongs to the query layer instead.
pitfalls: Date is an absolute instant while the business index is a calendar day: two Dates built from the same DateComponents in different TimeZones (or one via Calendar.startOfDay) are different instants, so day boundaries must be normalised explicitly (Calendar.startOfDay(for:) or a stored yyyy-MM-dd value).

Date() 'now' and the ambient TimeZone make the default accessor non-reproducible on devices and test simulators; pass the date (or a Calendar/TimeZone pair) in rather than reading the clock inside the model.

Arrays are value types with copy-on-write: mutating the history after it has been copied (for example passing it into a view model) triggers a full copy, and the sort on every put is O(n log n) - keep insertions ordered or maintain a separate sorted index when writes are frequent.

DateInterval expresses duration and has no open/closed bound semantics, so inclusive/exclusive rules at the boundaries of a validity period remain the caller's responsibility and are a classic off-by-one.
